draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: Beyond the counts, the survey data narrows the evidence further. Only eighteen voluntary shuttle riders completed the questionnaire, and no non-riders were included [@lyra:2]. These responses reflect the preferences of those already on the bus; they cannot establish demand across the broader student population [@lyra:2]. Without input from students who do not use the shuttle, the current metrics miss the views of those who might benefit from the service but have not yet ridden it. This absence means the pilot’s impact remains partially obscured. The available data confirms usage among a small, self-selected group but leaves the wider question of unmet need unresolved. I need to hear from non-riders before drawing conclusions about overall campus demand.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Because the survey omitted non-riders and no attendance data were collected, the pilot has not yet generated sufficient evidence to justify a permanent change [@lyra:2] [@lyra:1]. I propose extending the trial for one additional term specifically to close this gap. This temporary extension allows us to test the service under conditions where we can actively monitor who is using it and who is not. It provides a defined window to gather the missing perspectives without prematurely ending the trial based on incomplete information. The goal is not to assume the service succeeds or fails, but to create the necessary space for more rigorous data collection. By keeping the shuttle running for another term, the committee ensures that the next round of decisions rests on a clearer picture of actual access rather than on a sample that only captures existing riders.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: That second term must fix two measurement gaps before any final judgment. First, the survey team must include non-riders, since the current data only reflects the eighteen people who already chose to board [@lyra:2]. Without their input, we cannot tell whether low usage stems from service design or simple lack of awareness. Second, the data collection must explicitly separate boarding counts from class attendance, a distinction the pilot notes acknowledge is currently absent [@lyra:1]. This separation prevents us from mistakenly treating a rise in bus trips as proof of improved classroom engagement. I do not propose tracking costs or emissions, as no baseline for those metrics exists in the current record [@lyra:2]. Instead, the focus should remain on access: a brief survey question for non-riders and a parallel check of class registers would answer the specific question of who is actually being served. This added rigor costs little in effort but significantly increases the reliability of the data the committee will eventually review.
